# RAG, agents, and where they break {#sec-ch07}

::: {.epigraph by="Edsger W. Dijkstra, 1975"}
Simplicity is prerequisite for reliability.
:::

Ask an LLM what your company's backup account is allowed to do, and you'll get a confident, well-written, completely invented answer. It isn't lying; it has never seen your company's documents.

So we hand the model the right pages at the right moment, then give it tools and a loop so it can act. That's where most of today's AI excitement is, and most of the failures nobody notices. Watch for one pattern: nearly every weak point is a small decision.

::: {.goals}
- Explain the retrieve-then-generate pipeline, and why retrieval is the weak link.
- Describe an agent as an Observe, Decide, Act loop with tools, and count what it spends its steps on.
- Explain why errors add up over a loop.
- See how one planted sentence can steer a decision, and how trusted inputs stop it.
- Sketch the decision layer that catches most agent failures.
:::

## Give it the right page

Before the model answers, **search** your documents for the most relevant passages, **paste** them into the prompt, and **ask** it to answer from them. That's retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG. It works because every token the model writes depends on everything in its **context window**, the text it can read at once [@lewis2020].

![Retrieval-augmented generation. The question goes to a search step first, which pulls the most relevant chunks from your documents. The LLM sees the question plus those chunks, and answers from them, ideally citing which one it used.](/figures/ch12/pipeline.pdf){#fig-pipeline}

I built a small collection of {{< num ch12 n_docs int >}} company policies and guides, mixed with 300 old alerts that use the same words but answer nothing, the way real search indexes are full of near-misses. Asked "what is the backup account allowed to do?", the search put the right passage first {{< num ch12 recall.char.0 pct >}} of the time and in the top three {{< num ch12 recall.char.2 pct >}} of the time.

The part that decides whether RAG works isn't the LLM. If the passage with the answer isn't found, no model can use it, and the LLM builds the likeliest-sounding answer from what it *can* see: fluent, with a source, and wrong.

::: {.keyidea}
A RAG system can only be as good as its retrieval. Measure retrieval first.
:::

Some questions have no answer in the documents. A good system says "I don't know", and there's a simple signal for when: how well the *best* passage matches.

![The similarity of the best-matching chunk, for questions the knowledge base can answer (green, solid bars) and questions it can't (red, striped outline). They overlap, but not much. Below a threshold, the system should decline to answer.](/figures/ch12/abstain.pdf){#fig-abstain}

With the threshold where I've put it, the system answers {{< num ch12 answered_share pct >}} of answerable questions and only {{< num ch12 unans_answered pct >}} of unanswerable ones (@fig-abstain). Where the threshold should go depends on what a wrong answer costs, compared with an unnecessary "I don't know". That's Chapter 4's arithmetic.

Notice: a system built for *writing* answers turns on a small yes-or-no decision with a score and a threshold. So does deciding what an agent should remember, and which retrieved fact is reliable enough to act on.

## A model in a loop

Without the marketing, an **agent** is a model in a **loop**, with **tools**: look at the situation, decide what to do, do it, look again. Fighter pilots called it the OODA loop long before AI [@boyd1987]; I'll say **Observe, Decide, Act**.

A "tool call" sounds like the model pressing buttons. It doesn't. It *writes down* which tool it wants and with what arguments [@yao2023; @schick2023], and your code checks and runs it. That request is a choice from a fixed list plus some values: a typed decision wearing text. *The model suggests; your code decides.*

The book's security agent, for each alert, **decides** which evidence to gather, **decides** whether it has enough, **decides** the verdict, then acts: close the alert, write a note for a person, or wake someone up.

![What the agent spent its steps on, averaged over 300 alerts. Small typed decisions dominate. Free text, the thing LLMs are famous for, is a small minority of the work.](/figures/ch13/census.pdf){#fig-census}

Each alert took {{< num ch13 per_alert.decide f1 >}} small decisions, {{< num ch13 per_alert.observe f1 >}} tool reads, one action and {{< num ch13 per_alert.generate f2 >}} pieces of free text (@fig-census). Decisions were {{< num ch13 share_decide pct >}} of all steps; writing was {{< num ch13 share_generate pct >}}.

I built this agent, so I chose that mix. Count the steps of any agent you build or buy and I'd be surprised to see a different pattern: pick a tool, check a result, decide whether to continue, route the case. Writing happens now and then. Deciding is the everyday work.

::: {.keyidea}
Watch an agent work, and most of what it does is decide.
:::

## Errors add up

Loops bring uncomfortable arithmetic. If each step is right 95% of the time and a task needs ten steps, the task succeeds 0.95 × 0.95 × … ten times: about {{< num ch13 compound_95_10 pct >}}.

![The chance that every step of a task goes right, for different per-step reliabilities. Small per-step error rates become large task failure rates as the number of steps grows.](/figures/ch13/compound.pdf){#fig-compound}

That's why agents dazzle in demos and fail in real use (@fig-compound). A demo is a few steps on an easy case; real use is twenty steps on an odd one: {{< num ch13 compound_95_20 pct >}} at 95% per step. Decisions are most of the steps, so they're most of the risk. A decision that comes with a calibrated probability can be caught early and sent for review. One that comes back as a confident sentence can't.

::: {.keyidea}
Small errors multiply over a loop; calibrated doubt at each step is how you catch them.
:::

## Inputs can lie

The most dangerous failure: agents read text other people wrote (emails, tickets, web pages). An attacker who gets text in front of the model can plant instructions or false claims. That's **prompt injection** [@greshake2023], and it isn't only an LLM problem: any model that reads attacker-controlled text can be steered, decision models included.

Example. Some alerts say "Matches approved IT tooling (change ticket on file)", one of the strongest signs an alert is harmless. Suppose an attacker plants that sentence in a file name or email subject.

![How likely the decision model thinks each real threat is, reading the alert text as written (black, solid line) and with one planted sentence (red, dashed line). The sentence pulls many real threats below the auto-close threshold. When the same fact comes from a trusted system instead (green, dotted fill), the planted sentence does nothing.](/figures/ch14/injection.pdf){#fig-injection}

One sentence raised the share of real threats that would close unseen from {{< num ch14 inj_act_before pct >}} to {{< num ch14 inj_act_after pct >}} (@fig-injection). The fix is design, not a smarter model: ask the change-ticket system itself whether a ticket exists, and pass its answer as a separate field the attacker can't write. Then only {{< num ch14 inj_act_trusted pct >}} auto-close.

::: {.keyidea}
Take the facts that lower suspicion from systems attackers can't write to.
:::

Quieter failures: weak retrieval nobody checks ({{< num ch14 weak_retrieval pct >}} of the agent's lookups fell below the "I don't know" line), loops with no limit, and, worst, wrong actions at the end, like cutting the CEO's laptop off mid-meeting. Whenever anything goes wrong, from a timeout to a parse failure, send the case to a person, never act on it.

## The decision layer

Look back: nearly every protection in this chapter is the same thing, a check turned into a decision, with a threshold chosen from what mistakes cost.

![A decision layer between what an agent proposes and what actually happens: schema and allow-list checks, a typed decision with a calibrated probability, a threshold from costs, a budget and trusted facts, then one of three doors.](/figures/ch14/defences.pdf){#fig-defences}

The agent suggests; the **decision layer** decides (@fig-defences). It checks the suggestion against what's allowed, asks typed questions, applies cost-based thresholds and limits, takes risky facts from trusted systems, and sends each case through one of three doors: act, review or escalate.

None of that needs a smarter model. It needs decisions fast enough to use everywhere, cheap enough to ask often, and calibrated enough to put a threshold on. That's the gap a model like Jev is built for.

::: {.breaks}
Retrieved text is untrusted input. Keep instructions separate from data, and never let retrieved text start actions directly. A decision layer doesn't protect against everything, either. If the attacker controls a "trusted" system, the trusted field lies too. If every check has the same weakness, the layers all fail together. And thresholds set once and never checked again go out of date. Attack your own layer: try to get a real threat through the act door, and see which check stops you.
:::

::: {.threshold}
The agent can take four actions without a person: close an alert, add a note, block a sender domain, and cut a laptop off the network. Which should be allowed automatically when the model is confident, and which should always need a person?

(Closing and adding notes are cheap and can be undone, so they're fine automatically with a threshold on a calibrated probability. Blocking a domain can be undone but can cost business, so give it a stricter threshold and a list of partners it may never block. Cutting off a laptop stops someone's work and may destroy evidence, so it needs a person.)
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. Why doesn't retraining an LLM on your company's documents usually replace RAG? Give two practical reasons.
2. An agent vendor says their agent completes 90% of steps correctly, and a typical task is fifteen steps. What task success rate would you expect, and what else would you want to know?
3. Sketch an agent for a job you know. List its steps and label each as observe, decide, generate or act. What share are decisions?
:::
